title: NASA's 3,200-pound telescope to crash back to Earth in just hours
excerpt: NASA's doomed space telescope is expected to make an uncontrolled reentry back to Earth in the next few hours.
content:
NASA's 3,200-pound space telescope hurtles toward Earth with an uncontrolled crash in just hours

  • READ MORE: I worked with NASA. UFO disclosure will finally happen... but it's not coming from the White House

By STACY LIBERATORE, US SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY EDITOR

Published: 08:13 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 11:33 EDT, 4 November 2026

NASA's doomed space telescope is expected to make an uncontrolled reentry back to Earth in the next few hours.

The 3,200-pound Swift Observatory launched in 2004 to study gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe, and other cosmic objects and events. 

It was designed for a two-year prime mission. 

After 21 years of science operations, Swift’s low Earth orbit began to rapidly decay because of increased solar activity.

The latest predictions show that Swift is expected to reenter Earth’s atmosphere sometime on Wednesday. 

'Re-entry locations of any surviving components can vary from hemisphere to hemisphere and depend on when it re-enters,' NASA shared in a statement. 

 An updated tracking map shows Swift’s possible reentry paths sweeping over parts of Central and South America, Africa, South and Southeast Asia and northern Australia, as well as vast stretches of the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian oceans.

The map does not pinpoint where wreckage will strike, as the location of any surviving debris depends on exactly when the spacecraft plunges into the atmosphere and breaks apart.

The yellow and blue lines trace the telescope’s repeated passes around Earth. The map does not pinpoint where wreckage will strike

Pennsylvania State University’s John Nousek, an astronomer involved in the mission, told AP: 'We’ve known this day would come since before Swift was launched. 

'At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic.'

The space agency's press release explained that surviving fragments could fall within a broad belt around the equator stretching across parts of Latin America, Africa, southern Asia and northern Australia.

That places the US and Europe outside the potential impact zone. 

The re-entry follows NASA's failed attempt to rescue Swift in August.

The space agency had spent $30 million in hopes of sending another spacecraft to push the telescope into a higher orbit and avoid an uncontrolled fall back to Earth. 

 The rescue spacecraft, named Link, went into an uncontrollable spin a few weeks after its liftoff in early July.

While flight controllers managed to slow Link’s tumble, issues continued to plague its pointing and positioning in orbit.

The latest predictions show that Swift is expected to reenter Earth’s atmosphere sometime on Wednesday 

Swift Observatory captured the afterglow of a gamma-ray burst. The bright rings are X-rays scattered by dust layers within our galaxy. Multiple space and ground-based telescopes witnessed one of the brightest explosions in space when it reached Earth

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement: 'This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting.'

Swift resumed observations once the rescue attempt was called off, discovering even more gamma-ray bursts and other ultrahigh-energy events. But by late October, the telescope was too low to remain steady for observations, and its systems were shut down.

Its final tally included more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars, not to mention a slew of comets, asteroids and star-shredding black holes. 

The telescope’s superpower was its ability to swivel swiftly toward erupting celestial events.

NASA considered Swift a first responder for the Hubble and Webb space telescopes and others that would follow its alerts and provide deeper investigations. 

Scientists are still figuring out how to fill the gap.

Nousek said: 'Our fervent hope is that the lessons learned by the successes of Swift can be applied to new generations of space missions to accelerate our discoveries about the universe.'
